questions.q: Using the displayed cost graph, at what output does AVC reach its minimum?
questions.feedback: The AVC curve bottoms out where MC crosses it, at Q=25.

questions.q: Where does the average-cost curve reach its lowest point?
questions.feedback: The AC curve reaches its lowest point at Q=50.

questions.q: At Q=50 on the displayed graph, what is the vertical gap between AC and AVC?
questions.feedback: At Q=50, AC=$40 and AVC=$32, so the gap—and AFC—is $8.

questions.q: At Q=25 on the displayed graph, what marginal cost is indicated by the MC–AVC intersection?
questions.feedback: The MC and AVC curves meet at Q=25 and cost $30.

questions.q: At Q=50 on the displayed graph, what marginal cost is indicated by the MC–AC intersection?
questions.feedback: MC crosses AC at Q=50 and $40.

questions.q: Use the values at Q=50 on the displayed graph. What total fixed cost is implied?
questions.feedback: AFC=AC−AVC=$8 at Q=50, so TFC=$8×50=$400.

questions.q: Inspect the curves around Q=35. As output rises slightly from that point, which pattern is consistent with the graph?
questions.feedback: Around Q=35, MC lies above AVC but below AC, so it pulls AVC up and AC down.

questions.q: Inspect the curves just to the right of Q=50. What happens to both average-cost curves as output increases?
questions.feedback: Beyond Q=50, MC lies above both averages, so both are pulled upward.

questions.q: Inspect the low-output region to the left of Q=25. Which movement of the average-cost curves is consistent with the graph?
options: Both AC and AVC are falling
Both AC and AVC are rising together
AC rises while AVC continues falling
AC is flat while AVC continues rising
questions.feedback: Before the AVC minimum, MC is below the average curves, pulling them downward.

questions.q: The graph implies TFC from the AC–AVC gap at Q=50. With that same TFC, what would AFC be at Q=25?
questions.feedback: The Q=50 gap implies TFC=$400. At Q=25, AFC=$400/25=$16.

questions.q: Use the graph to infer TFC at Q=50. If output later rises to 100 units with TFC unchanged, what would AFC be?
questions.feedback: The graph implies TFC=$400, so at Q=100, AFC=$400/100=$4.

questions.q: For an output between the AVC minimum and the AC minimum shown, which ordering of AVC, MC, and AC is consistent with the graph?
questions.feedback: After MC crosses AVC but before it crosses AC, MC is above AVC and below AC.

questions.q: On the displayed graph, at what output does AVC reach $10 at its minimum?
questions.feedback: AVC bottoms out at Q=200 and $10.

questions.q: On the displayed graph, at what output is AC minimized?
questions.feedback: AC reaches its minimum at Q=400.

questions.q: At Q=400, what AVC value is marked on the displayed graph?
questions.feedback: The marked AVC value at Q=400 is $12.

questions.q: At Q=200, what value does the MC–AVC intersection show?
questions.feedback: MC equals AVC at the AVC minimum, $10 at Q=200.

questions.q: At Q=400, what value does the MC–AC intersection show?
questions.feedback: MC and AC meet at $20 when Q=400.

questions.q: At Q=400, what does the displayed AC–AVC gap imply for AFC?
questions.feedback: At Q=400, AC=$20 and AVC=$12, so AFC=$8.

questions.q: At about Q=300, inspect the position of MC relative to AVC and AC. Which movement of the averages follows as output rises?
questions.feedback: Between the two minima, MC is above AVC but below AC.

questions.q: Immediately to the right of the AC minimum near Q=400, what does the graph imply?
options: MC is below AC, so AC rises
MC is above AVC, so AVC falls
MC equals AFC, so AC is flat
MC is above AC, so AC rises
questions.feedback: Past the AC minimum, MC lies above AC and pulls it upward.

questions.q: Use the marked values at Q=400. What total fixed cost is implied by the graph?
questions.feedback: AFC is $20−$12=$8; multiplying by 400 units gives TFC=$3,200.

questions.q: Infer TFC from the Q=400 values. With the same TFC, what is AFC at Q=200?
questions.feedback: The graph implies TFC=$3,200, so AFC at Q=200 is $16.

questions.q: At Q=200, the graph shows AVC=$10. Using the TFC implied by the Q=400 gap, what AC would correspond to Q=200?
questions.feedback: TFC=$3,200 gives AFC=$16 at Q=200; AC=AVC+AFC=$10+$16=$26.

questions.q: Using the Q=400 values as the baseline, suppose fixed cost doubles while the variable-cost schedule is unchanged. What would AC be at Q=400?
questions.feedback: Baseline AFC is $8. Doubling fixed cost doubles AFC to $16, while AVC stays $12; AC becomes $28.

questions.q: At Q=120, which labeled point lies on the total-cost curve?
questions.feedback: At Q=120, total cost is the upper curve at Point A ($1,200).

questions.q: Which labeled point marks $800 of variable cost when output is 120 units?
questions.feedback: Point B marks TVC=$800 at Q=120.

questions.q: The horizontal $400 fixed-cost line passes through which labeled point at Q=120?
questions.feedback: Point C lies on the horizontal TFC line at $400.

questions.q: At Q=120, what is the vertical distance between Points A and B?
questions.feedback: The gap is $1,200−$800=$400, equal to TFC.

questions.q: Use Point A at Q=120. What is average total cost at that output?
Use Point B at Q=120. Approximately what is average variable cost?
Use Point C at Q=120. Approximately what is average fixed cost?
The graph shows the upper and middle curves staying a constant vertical distance apart. Which fact explains that pattern?
options: Both curves are measures of fixed cost
Variable cost is constant at every output
Their difference is the constant TFC
questions.feedback: TC−TVC=TFC, and TFC is constant in the short run.

questions.q: At zero output, what explains the vertical gap between the total-cost and variable-cost curves?
questions.feedback: Fixed cost is incurred even when output is zero.

questions.q: Use the horizontal TFC line and the marked output of 200 units. What average fixed cost is implied?
At Q=120, what percentage of total cost is variable cost, using Points A and B?
At Q=120, suppose variable input costs raise TVC by 25% while TFC is unchanged. What new pair of totals follows from the graph?
questions.feedback: TVC rises from $800 to $1,000; adding unchanged TFC=$400 gives TC=$1,400.

questions.q: At Q=120, suppose TFC rises from $400 to $600 while the variable-cost curve is unchanged. Approximately what would ATC become?
At the marked output Q = 120, which cost identity is demonstrated by points A, B, and C?
questions.feedback: $1,200=$800+$400, illustrating TC=TVC+TFC.

questions.q: At about how many workers does total product reach its highest point on the graph?
questions.feedback: The TP curve peaks at about 10 workers.

questions.q: Approximately how much total product is produced at the peak of the displayed curve?
questions.feedback: The peak occurs at roughly 150 units of total product.

questions.q: At the labor input where the displayed total-product curve reaches its maximum, what is marginal product?
questions.feedback: At the peak of TP, the slope of TP—and therefore MP—is zero.

questions.q: For labor inputs to the right of the total-product maximum, what sign does marginal product have?
questions.feedback: A downward-sloping TP curve means each added worker reduces total output, so MP is negative.

questions.q: Use the shape of total product between about 6 and 9 workers. Which description of marginal product fits that region?
options: MP is positive and increasing throughout
questions.feedback: TP still rises, so MP is positive; the flattening slope shows MP is decreasing.

questions.q: Use the portion of the total-product curve after its maximum. Which combination of total product and marginal product is consistent with the graph?
options: TP rises and MP is negative
TP falls and MP is positive
TP is constant and MP is positive
TP falls and MP is negative
questions.feedback: The falling TP curve after its peak means marginal product is negative.

questions.q: Which visual feature shows that diminishing marginal product begins before total product starts falling?
options: TP begins flattening while it is still rising
TP starts at zero before any labor is used
TP eventually turns downward after the peak at the shown output
The peak occurs at approximately 150 units
questions.feedback: Diminishing MP appears when TP’s positive slope starts shrinking, before TP reaches its maximum.

questions.q: At the total-product maximum, use the labeled output and labor input to calculate average product.
questions.feedback: AP=TP/L=150/10=15, even though MP is zero at the TP maximum.

questions.q: Move one worker beyond the total-product maximum. Which pair of statements must be true?
options: The 11th worker has positive MP, while AP has fallen to zero
The 11th worker has zero MP, while AP has become negative
The 11th worker has negative MP, while AP remains positive
Both MP and AP must already be negative at 11 workers
questions.feedback: A decline in TP makes the 11th worker’s MP negative, but positive total output divided by 11 keeps AP positive.

questions.q: Checkpoint: Use the total-product curve to correct the claim that “TP is maximized where MP is maximized.”
options: TP is maximized where MP first becomes positive
TP is maximized where AP equals zero
TP is maximized where fixed cost is minimized
TP is maximized where MP falls to zero
questions.feedback: TP reaches its peak when its slope, MP, equals zero—not when MP itself is highest.

questions.q: Which curve reaches its peak at the lower labor input in the displayed graph?
options: They peak at the same labor input
questions.feedback: The MP curve peaks before the AP curve.

questions.q: At about how many workers do MP and AP intersect?
questions.feedback: The curves cross at about seven workers.

questions.q: At about 5 workers, how is MP positioned relative to AP on the graph?
options: MP is negative while AP is positive
questions.feedback: Near five workers, the red MP curve lies above the green AP curve.

questions.q: At about 9 workers, which comparison matches the graph?
options: MP is above AP and remains positive
MP equals AP at that labor input
MP is negative while AP remains at zero
MP is below AP but still positive
questions.feedback: Near nine workers, MP is positive but lies below AP.

questions.q: Near 10 workers, what happens to MP on the displayed graph?
options: MP equals the peak of AP
MP becomes equal to total product
questions.feedback: The MP curve crosses the horizontal axis at about ten workers.

questions.q: At the marked labor input where MP lies above AP, what should happen to AP when another worker is added?
questions.feedback: A marginal value above the average pulls the average upward.

questions.q: At the marked labor input where MP is below AP but still positive, what happens to TP and AP as another worker is added?
options: TP is constant while AP rises
questions.feedback: Positive MP raises TP, but MP below AP pulls AP downward.

questions.q: At the point where the MP and AP curves intersect, what is true of average product?
options: MP is at its own maximum
questions.feedback: An average is maximized where the marginal value crosses it from above.

questions.q: Just to the right of the point where MP crosses zero, how should the positive AP reading and the shape of TP be interpreted together?
options: TP is declining even though output per worker remains positive
TP must keep rising whenever AP remains positive at the shown output
TP must fall all the way to zero when MP is zero
AP must immediately become negative once MP does
questions.feedback: Negative MP lowers total product, while positive TP divided by labor can leave AP positive.

questions.q: Inspect the MP–AP crossing near 7 workers. What happens to AP immediately before versus immediately after that crossing?
options: AP falls both before and after the crossing
AP rises before the crossing and falls after it
AP rises both before and after the crossing
AP remains at zero on both sides of the crossing
questions.feedback: MP is above AP before the crossing and below AP afterward, so AP changes from rising to falling.

questions.q: Compare the locations of the MP peak and AP peak. What does their ordering demonstrate about marginal and average product?
options: AP must immediately fall as soon as MP begins to decline
MP can fall only after AP has already become negative
A falling marginal can still raise the average while it remains above the average
The marginal-average relationship does not apply to product measures at the shown output
questions.feedback: MP can decline yet remain above AP; while it does, AP continues to rise.

questions.q: At the labor input near the TP maximum, use the displayed AP value to infer total product.
questions.feedback: TP=AP×L≈15×10=150 units.

questions.q: Checkpoint: At the MP–AP intersection, what is happening to AP?
questions.feedback: AP is maximized where MP crosses AP from above.

questions.q: Checkpoint: In the region where MP is below AP but still positive, which product measure has already passed its maximum while total product has not?
questions.feedback: When MP is below AP, AP is falling and has already passed its peak; because MP is still positive, TP is still rising.

questions.q: At what output does the displayed LRAC curve reach its minimum?
questions.feedback: The LRAC curve bottoms out at Q=60.

questions.q: Approximately what LRAC does the graph show at Q=30?
questions.feedback: At Q=30, the curve is near the $20 gridline.

questions.q: Read LRAC at the higher marked output, Q = 90. What value is shown?
questions.feedback: At Q=90, the curve is again near $20.

questions.q: If a firm expands output from about 30 toward 60 units, what happens to LRAC on the displayed curve?
options: LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale
LRAC falls, indicating diseconomies of scale
questions.feedback: The left side of the U-shaped LRAC slopes downward toward its minimum.

questions.q: If a firm expands output from about 60 toward 90 units, what happens to LRAC?
options: LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale at the shown output
LRAC stays at the minimum of about $12
LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
LRAC rises, indicating economies of scale
questions.feedback: To the right of the minimum, LRAC rises as scale expands.

questions.q: The graph gives roughly the same LRAC at Q=30 and Q=90. Which statement distinguishes those two positions?
options: Expanding from either output lowers LRAC at the same rate at the shown output
Expanding from either output raises LRAC at the same rate
LRAC stays flat throughout the interval from Q=30 to Q=90
Expanding from Q=30 lowers LRAC, while expanding from Q=90 raises LRAC
questions.feedback: Q=30 lies on the economies-of-scale side; Q=90 lies on the diseconomies side.

questions.q: A firm currently produces 30 units at an LRAC of about $20. According to the graph, which move most directly approaches minimum efficient scale?
options: Remain at 30 because LRAC is already minimized
questions.feedback: The minimum occurs at Q=60, so moving from 30 toward 60 approaches MES.

questions.q: Two firms have similar LRAC: one operates near Q=30 and the other near Q=90. If each increases output slightly, what does the graph predict?
options: Both firms’ LRAC falls as output expands slightly
The first firm’s LRAC falls; the second firm’s LRAC rises
Both firms’ LRAC rises as output expands slightly
The first firm’s LRAC rises while the second firm’s LRAC falls
questions.feedback: The firms are on opposite sides of the LRAC minimum at Q=60.

questions.q: What output is the minimum efficient scale represented by this graph?
questions.feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining minimum LRAC; here that point is Q=60.

questions.q: Which claim is NOT supported by the shape of the displayed LRAC curve?
options: LRAC falls as output approaches 60 from the left side at the shown output
LRAC rises as output moves above 60 on the right side
The minimum LRAC occurs at approximately Q=60
There is a broad flat interval of constant returns to scale
questions.feedback: The graph has a single rounded minimum rather than a visibly flat minimum-cost interval.
